title: Jelly Roll Morton notes, Handy and the junk men's horns
summary: Russell starts through his Morton notes: the Handy dispute and junk men's horns; what is already at Tulane.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: We're going through the Jelly Roll Morton. I can't talk at all sometimes. The Jelly notes in my notebook. First of all, I have a lot of things copied, like that big letter he wrote, the downbeat, and also the Afro-American in Baltimore. When Handy wrote an article saying he had invented the blues, and Jelly told him he'd heard more blues back here on the old junk man's horn than Handy would ever know. Incidentally, Johnny Wiggs' interview, he raved about those junk men, which I guess we'll never get to know now. The great big long horn, like a New Year's horn, that they'd play the blues on. They must have been terrific, because Johnny's never forgotten. The only other person that ever rivaled them was Joe Oliver, according to Johnny, which is about as high praise as Johnny can make.
Do we have copies of this material here?
We must have, if Mrs. Rankin or somebody can check on, if we don't have this Jelly letter in the old downbeat, if it's republished in downbeat, we must have it.
All right, don't waste any more time on that.
And Handy, yeah, sure. I don't know, I've been through those things.

Yeah, so many people talk to Jelly, and there's so much stuff written in that Lomax book, which has a lot of wonderful material in it, as well as all the Library of Congress, so I don't want to waste a lot of time going over this.
